You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Loophole and Drafting Review: S. 2817 (Manager's Amendment, Oct. 6, 2026)

I reviewed the text you provided. I can't check the U.S. Code or the introduced version from here, so verify the statutory references noted below and compare against the introduced text to see what the manager's amendment changed.

## Definitions (§2)

1. **§2(1)(A), "by a single vessel":** The 10,000-ton threshold applies per vessel, so an operator could split recovery across several vessels that each stay under it. Consider an operator-level or aggregate test.

2. **§2(1)(A), "per year":** The bill doesn't specify whether this means a calendar or rolling year, how partial years are handled, or how ramp-up and pilot phases are treated. It also doesn't say whether the tonnage is wet or dry weight, or whether discarded material counts as "recovery."

3. **§2(1)(A), "other mineral resources":** This term is undefined. It's unclear whether it covers polymetallic sulfides, cobalt crusts, phosphorites, or sand and gravel.

4. **§2(1)(A), "depths greater than 200 meters":** This excludes all shallower seabed, including the continental shelf. Confirm that exclusion is intended, since it leaves significant seabed mining outside the prohibition. The bill also doesn't say how depth is measured for a vessel working across varying depths.

5. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary":** No Secretary is defined. Section 6 refers to the Secretary of State, and Section 4 names NOAA, so readers can't tell which official makes the §2(1)(B) determination.

6. **§2(1)(B), "poses risks... comparable":** The bill sets no standard for comparability and no procedure (notice, comment, record, judicial review) for the determination. That invites both agency delay and challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act.

7. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** This definition excludes LLCs, partnerships, and trusts. "State" is also undefined, so it's unclear whether DC and territories count. Because §3(a) reaches "any U.S. person anywhere," a U.S. parent could operate through an LLC or other unlisted entity and fall outside the definition.

8. **§2(3), "covered vessel" and "equipped for":** "Equipped" is undefined, and the 5,000 gross ton threshold uses a different unit than the 10,000 metric ton threshold, which is a source of confusion.

9. **Definitions mismatch (§2(1), §2(3), §4):** The §3 prohibition is keyed to activity thresholds, but the §4 registry and reporting duties apply only to "covered vessels" over 5,000 GT. A smaller vessel doing commercial mining would be prohibited but never registered or reported, so NOAA would have no visibility into it.

## Prohibition (§3)

10. **§3(a), "engage in":** This term is undefined. It's unclear whether it covers financing, chartering, supplying equipment, processing, exporting nodules, or investing. A U.S. firm supplying services to a foreign miner could argue it isn't "engaging in" mining.

11. **§3(a), "in the United States":** The bill doesn't say whether this includes the Exclusive Economic Zone and continental shelf, where much seabed mining would take place. It also leaves unclear how far the prohibition reaches beyond U.S. jurisdiction, given that the seabed beyond national jurisdiction falls under separate international rules.

12. **§3(b), "exploration license":** The bill doesn't name the licensing statute. It also doesn't say that an exploration license does not authorize commercial recovery, which leaves room for an operator to argue that commercial mining is "conducted under" such a license.

13. **§3(b), grandfathering scope:** The bill doesn't limit renewals, amendments, area expansions, transfers, or extended terms of licenses issued before enactment. It also doesn't require that a grandfathered license be valid and in good standing. As I understand the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. §1401 et seq.), that law also provides commercial recovery permits, and the bill doesn't mention them, so verify whether any pending applications or permits fall outside the exemption.

14. **§3(c), environmental assessment (largest loophole):** This exemption has no limit on volume, duration, revenue, equipment, or disposition of material. An operator could conduct commercial-scale recovery and label it an "environmental assessment." At minimum, the exemption needs a volume cap, advance notice or approval, a time limit, and a bar on selling recovered material.

15. **§3(c) and §2(1):** The bill doesn't say whether assessment activities still count toward the recovery thresholds in §2(1)(A). Without that, the thresholds could be avoided by labeling activity as assessment.

## Registry and Reporting (§4)

16. **§4(a), "operator":** This term is undefined. The bill also sets no registration deadline, no timing relative to the effective date, no required content, and no specific NOAA office or process.

17. **§4(b), quarterly reports:** Required content is limited to "describing recovery activities." The bill doesn't require quantities, locations, depths, or discharges, sets no due dates, makes no reports public, and provides no verification of the operator's certification.

18. **§4 has no penalty (significant enforcement gap):** Section 5 penalizes only violations of §3. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false report carries no express consequence under this bill.

19. **No enforcement tools in §§2–4:** The bill gives no inspection or boarding authority, no vessel monitoring requirement, no data-access rights, and no rulemaking authority for the Secretary to implement the definitions or the registry.

## Penalties and Enforcement (§5)

20. **§5(a), "for each day":** The unit of violation is undefined (per vessel, per ton, per operation, or per day), and a continuing operation could be counted day after day.

21. **§5(a) and §8, effective dates:** §5(a) applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 delays the Act's effective date by 180 days. This creates ambiguity about whether penalties can accrue during that gap. Confirm the intended result.

22. **§5, enforcement mechanics:** The bill doesn't name an enforcing agency or court, provide for injunctive relief, authorize vessel seizure or forfeiture, or create a citizen-suit provision. It also doesn't address inflation adjustment, a statute of limitations, or liability for corporate officers.

23. **§5(b), "willfully":** This term is undefined. Also, the imprisonment provision reaches individuals, but the bill doesn't say how corporate liability is handled beyond fines.

## International Agreement (§6)

24. **§6, "shall seek to negotiate":** This is a procedural obligation only. The bill doesn't require the Secretary to report on progress, sets no consequence for failure, and doesn't define "equivalent to" the §3 prohibitions. It also doesn't address how the agreement would relate to the International Seabed Authority or the U.S. position on UNCLOS.

## Duration and Sunset (§7)

25. **§7(a) and §7(b) conflict (high priority):** §7(a) keeps the §3 prohibition in effect until Congress passes a joint resolution, while §7(b) ends the entire Act 10 years after enactment. The bill doesn't say which controls, so a court or agency could read either way. Clarify whether the sunset applies to the prohibition.

26. **§7(a), NASEM report:** Nothing requires the National Academies to produce a report, sets a deadline, or defines the report's scope. If no report is produced, the joint-resolution mechanism can't operate as written.

27. **§7(a), "serious harm":** This standard is undefined, and the bill doesn't say who decides whether it's met beyond Congress's finding.

28. **§7(a), joint resolution:** The bill doesn't say whether presentment to the President applies. It also doesn't say whether expedited procedures apply. Standard practice would send a joint resolution to the President, so the text should say so explicitly.

29. **§7(b), no savings clause:** Nothing preserves accrued penalties, pending enforcement actions, or obligations incurred before the sunset date.

## General Structure

30. **No conflict or savings clause with existing law:** The bill doesn't say how it interacts with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, or other regimes. That invites conflict and implied-repeal arguments.

31. **No severability clause:** If a key provision (such as the §2(1)(B) determination or the §7 sunset) is struck, courts would apply default presumptions to decide what survives. A severability clause would reduce that uncertainty.

## Suggested Priorities for Thursday's Markup

- **§3(c)** environmental-assessment exemption (item 14)
- **§7(a) vs. §7(b)** sunset conflict (item 25)
- **§4 with no penalty** (item 18)
- **§3(b)** grandfathering scope (items 12–13)
- **"Single vessel" and "U.S. person"** definitions (items 1, 7)
- **§3(a) territorial reach** (item 11)

If it would help, I can draft a one-page summary for the story or a list of plain-language questions for committee staff.
